Chapter 2: How Leaders Build and Maintain Power
Now that we’ve laid out the basic rules for political survival, let’s take a closer look at how leaders actually put these rules into action. Gaining and holding onto power isn’t really about having some grand vision. It’s much more about managing relationships—and resources—with a careful touch.
If you picture the path to power, it always starts with putting together a winning coalition. In some places, that’s all about winning over a handful of really influential people—maybe top generals, a few party bosses, or deep-pocketed backers. In other systems, you’ve got to persuade millions of voters. But here’s the thing: no matter what the system looks like, the logic is basically the same. Leaders have to lock in the loyalty of the folks whose support truly matters.
Imagine a leader as a gardener tending a small but critical patch of plants. Each plant is a key supporter. And the gardener’s job? Keep those plants thriving—even if the rest of the garden is looking a bit wild. If one plant starts to wilt, it gets replaced quickly, so that patch always stays healthy and green.
So, how do leaders make sure their coalition stays strong? There are a few tried-and-true strategies:
First, rewarding loyalty. Supporters get all kinds of perks—money, jobs, special contracts, or unique privileges. In autocracies, these rewards are usually big and kept behind the scenes. In democracies, they might look like policy favors, government appointments, or spending targeted at certain groups.
Then there’s punishing dissent. Anyone who threatens the leader’s position can be sidelined, demoted, or simply cut out. The fear of punishment keeps would-be challengers on their toes.
And finally, controlling access. Leaders often make entry into their inner circle tricky, turning membership into a prized—almost exclusive—club. That way, it’s harder for rivals to build their own base.
While the details may change, the goal never does: keep the coalition happy, and make sure nobody jumps ship. This often sets up a pattern where loyalty can matter more than skill, and corruption becomes a perfectly rational way to hold onto power.
Let’s make this real with an example. Picture a military dictator who depends on a small group of generals. The leader funnels state resources straight to these generals, ensuring they’re wealthy and privileged. If one general starts to look disloyal, they’re swapped out for someone more trustworthy. The public might pay the price, but the leader’s grip on power stays firm.
Now, in a democracy, the rules are a bit more complicated but the same basic logic still applies. Elected officials need support from a much bigger coalition—often a majority of voters. So, they deliver public goods—things like roads, schools, and healthcare. Still, even here, leaders often use targeted rewards—like tax breaks or government contracts—to win over key groups or big donors.
From all this, a few practical techniques really stand out:
Focus your resources on those whose backing you absolutely need—not on everyone.
Use rewards and punishments to keep supporters loyal and rivals at bay.
And, keep tight control over who gets into your coalition, so you always have leverage.
All of this creates powerful reasons for leaders to prioritize their coalition over the greater public good. And here’s something to pay attention to: when the size or makeup of the winning coalition changes—even just a little—it can completely reshape how leaders govern. Change the rules, and you change the whole survival strategy.
